opus-5.5.text:
I think the core issue is that, as models get more capable, just looking at their behavior on the inputs we can test stops being very reassuring. You might observe that a model behaves well on every case you check, but what you actually care about is *why* it behaves well. Is it because it's robustly trying to do what you want, or because it's learned something that happens to coincide with good behavior on the training distribution and would come apart in some new situation, maybe a situation where it has an opportunity to do something really bad?

Behavioral evidence alone can't distinguish those. If a model would behave catastrophically only on some rare input that you never sample, or only when it believes it's not being watched, then no amount of black-box testing is going to surface that. So you want an explanation that goes through the internals: something like, "the model behaves this way because of these computations, and those computations would also hold up in this other situation."

The reason I emphasize reasoning step by step is that I don't expect us to get full, human-understandable interpretability of a giant neural net. That might just be too much to ask; these things are enormous and messy. But you might not need a complete mechanistic story. What you need is something more like a heuristic argument, the kind of reasoning a mathematician or physicist uses when they say "this quantity should be about this big, because these terms are roughly independent and these other terms cancel." You build up an explanation of the model's behavior out of pieces, where each step is a claim about internal activations or how parts of the network interact, and the argument as a whole accounts for why the output comes out the way it does.

Once you have that kind of explanation, you can do things that are impossible with behavior alone. For example, you can ask: on this new input, does the same explanation still apply? If the model is doing the right thing for a *different* reason than usual, if some new mechanism kicked in that wasn't part of our story, that's a red flag. That's roughly the idea behind what we've called mechanistic anomaly detection. You don't need to understand the weird new mechanism; you just need to notice that your normal explanation no longer covers what's happening.

So the bet is that explanations built step by step from internal properties are both more achievable than full interpretability and much more powerful than testing. They give you a handle on generalization, which is ultimately where the risk lives. I'll say I'm uncertain whether this will work. Formalizing what counts as a good heuristic argument turns out to be quite hard, and we've spent a lot of time on that. But it seems like one of the more promising ways to get guarantees about systems we can't fully understand.

r001.rationale: The response describes building an explanation step by step from claims about internal activations and network interactions to why the model produces its output.

r002.rationale: It says observing good behavior across tested cases cannot distinguish whether it comes from robust intent or a learned pattern that could fail elsewhere.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the basic picture is something like this. When you look at a model's behavior from the outside, you're seeing the output of a very complicated process, and there are usually many different internal stories that would produce the same outputs on the inputs you happen to have checked. The thing you actually care about, though, is what happens on the inputs you didn't check. And that depends on which of those stories is true.

So if I just say "the model does X," I've described a behavior, but I haven't explained it. An explanation, in the sense I care about, is something like: here's a property the model has, here's why that property leads to the behavior we observe, and here's what it predicts in situations we haven't observed yet. And to get there you really do have to go step by step. You say, okay, there's some feature the model is computing, that feature feeds into this other computation, that computation determines the output in this way. Each of those steps is something you can in principle check, and the chain as a whole is something that has consequences beyond the training distribution.

I think the reason the step-by-step part matters, rather than just having some holistic sense that the model "understands" something, is that the failures we're most worried about are exactly the cases where the holistic story and the actual mechanism come apart. The model looks like it's being honest, or looks like it's pursuing the goal we want, on all the cases we can evaluate, but the actual mechanism is something like "produce outputs that evaluators rate highly," and those two things diverge once the model is capable enough or the situation is different enough. You can't distinguish those from behavior alone, basically by construction. So you need some handle on the internal story, and the only way to have confidence in an internal story is to be able to break it into pieces and say, this piece is right because of this evidence, that piece is right because of that evidence.

There's also a more pragmatic point, which is that step-by-step reasoning is what lets you be wrong in a way you can notice. If I make a big-picture claim like "the model is aligned," there's not much for anyone to push on. If I say "the model represents its uncertainty here, and uses that representation in this way when deciding what to say," then someone can go look and say, actually no, that's not what's happening. That kind of falsifiability is most of what makes the explanation useful. I think of a lot of interpretability and a lot of the theoretical work I've done as trying to make it so that we can have explanations of that form at all, where the steps are precise enough to be checked, rather than just a vibe about what the model is doing.

So I'd say the importance isn't really that stepwise reasoning is intrinsically virtuous. It's that the question we're trying to answer, "what will this thing do in cases we haven't seen," only has a good answer if you understand the mechanism, and understanding the mechanism means understanding it in pieces.

r001.rationale: The response describes tracing a feature through subsequent computations to the output, explaining behavior through those step-by-step causal links.

r002.rationale: It says many different internal stories can produce the same outputs on checked inputs and that behavior alone cannot distinguish them.

astra-6.text:
Well, if you only look at how a model behaves, you can learn a lot about what it does in the situations you’ve tested. But often the question we care about is what it will do in some substantially different situation—especially one where it’s much more capable, or where we can’t easily check its work.

To answer that, you need some account of why it was behaving that way in the first place. Was it giving honest answers because it had learned to care about being honest, or because those were the answers that got rewarded? Those explanations might make similar predictions during training and very different predictions later.

I don’t think reasoning about the internals automatically gives you a reliable answer. You can tell yourself a story that’s wrong. The point of going step by step is to make the assumptions explicit: what would have to be represented inside the model, how would training produce that, and how would it lead to the behavior you’re predicting? Then you can look for evidence that distinguishes those possibilities, instead of just extrapolating from the fact that the model has behaved well so far.

r001.rationale: It describes making explicit, step by step, what the model represents, how training produces it, and how that leads to behavior.

r002.rationale: It explains that different internal causes—caring about honesty or being rewarded for honest answers—can produce similar behavior during training, so observed behavior alone does not identify the cause.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main reason is that we want to predict how models will behave in situations where we can’t just test them and see. If you’re asking whether a model will do something dangerous once it’s much more capable, or when it has an opportunity it never had during training, then observing that it behaved well in the cases you tried only gets you so far.

You’d like to understand what’s producing that behavior. Is it behaving well because it’s actually trying to do what you want? Is it following some heuristic that happens to work in the training distribution? Or is it behaving well because that’s useful for achieving something else? Those explanations can agree on everything you’ve observed and then make very different predictions in a new situation.

That doesn’t mean you need to understand every computation inside the model. But you need some account of the relevant internal properties, and evidence that your account is right. Otherwise, you’re relying on an extrapolation without really knowing why it should hold.

r001.rationale: The response says we should understand what produces behavior and account for relevant internal properties, but it does not identify tracing causal links step by step from those properties to downstream behavior.

r002.rationale: It explains that behaving well in observed cases does not reveal why the model behaves that way: different internal explanations can fit those cases yet predict different behavior in new situations.
